summary: A request from SRI-ARC to network liaisons for mailbox addresses, because the NIC was about to start delivering Journal articles to users who wanted them. Delivery could be online at the NIC, by postal hardcopy, or by network mail to a home host, using FTP's mail commands.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 510 asks network liaisons to collect mailbox addresses and delivery preferences. The NIC needed those details to send Network Journal material to interested users.

questions: how did the nic deliver journal articles
what delivery options existed for network journal
subtitle: A request for mailbox details so the NIC could deliver its Network Journal by network mail.

tldr.problem: The NIC planned to offer Network Journal delivery, but needed each interested user's delivery preferences and network mailbox address.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 510 asks network liaisons to provide each user's NIC Ident, delivery choices, destination host and the user name required by that host's FTP server.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes a planned service and requests the information needed to configure it; it is not the service specification.

today: The unit records RFC 510's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. The memo requests information for a planned Network Journal delivery service.

sections.title: Planned Journal Delivery
sections.content:
The NIC planned to begin delivering Network Journal material to users who wanted it. Users could choose online delivery to the AUTHOR branch of their initial file at the NIC, hardcopy by postal service, or network delivery to a mailbox on their home host. They could choose any or all of these modes.

The RFC is a request for information, not documentation of the service. The author says that a service description would be written once it became available.
sections.plainLanguage: The NIC planned three ways to deliver Journal material: online, on paper, or to a network mailbox. This memo asks for setup details before describing the service itself.

sections.title: How Network Mail Would Work
sections.content:
For network delivery, FTP mail commands would send mail to a host and mailbox chosen by the user. Each message would include a header with information such as the author's NIC Ident, submission date and title. It would contain the message text or, for long material, a pointer to the text.

For bulk mail, an FTP user process acting for the recipient could use the pointer to retrieve the text from SRI-ARC. The pathname would cause the FTP server to convert the file from NLS's tree-structured form to sequential form before sending it.
sections.plainLanguage: Short material could arrive in the mail message itself. For long material, the message could point to a file that the recipient retrieves from SRI-ARC.

sections.title: Information Requested from Liaisons
sections.content:
For every user affiliated with their host organization who wanted network delivery, liaisons were asked to send four details: the user's NIC Ident; any additional delivery modes desired; the standard host name or decimal host address; and the user name required by that host's FTP server for a mail command.

The NIC would store the delivery host and mailbox in its Ident file. Users could view or change this information, along with their delivery modes, through the Identification System in NLS. The memo asks liaisons to provide the information for interested users at their host, while also accepting it from others.
sections.plainLanguage: The NIC needs a user's identifier, delivery choices, destination computer and account name for that computer. It would keep these settings in the user's Ident file.
